In the figure above, $\overset{\to }{OC}$ is the bisector of $∠AOB.$ If $m∠AOB={58}^{∘}$, find $m∠AOC.$
questions.worked_solution:
The bisector of an angle divides the angle into two congruent angles. Each of these congruent angles has a measure that is half the measure of the larger bisected angle. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AOC & =\frac{m∠AOB}{2} \\  & =\frac{{58}^{∘}}{2} \\  & ={29}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191213/assets/19334b594e8567464103bacc4f0978cbbbc664c3cc5a1a6edd5789e822030c4b.png)

Let $m∠COD=x$ and $m∠EOC=y.$ Then,

$$
m∠EOD=m∠COD+m∠EOC=x+y.
$$

Since $\overset{⟶}{OD}$ is a bisector of $∠COA,$ we have

$$
m∠COA=2x.
$$

Since $\overset{⟶}{OE}$ is a bisector of $∠BOC,$ we have

$$
m∠BOC=2y.
$$

Finally, since $∠AOB$ is a straight angle, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠COA+m∠BOC & =m∠AOB \\ 2x+2y & ={180}^{∘} \\ x+y & ={90}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $m∠EOD=x+y={90}^{∘}.$

In the figure above, $\overset{\to }{OD}$ and $\overset{\to }{OE}$ are the bisectors of $∠AOC$ and $∠BOC,$ respectively. If $m∠DOC=x,$ $m∠COE=2x+{2}^{∘},$ and $m∠AOB={130}^{∘},$ find the value of $m∠BOC.$
questions.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191213/assets/484a70ad0c9eeca1ea03db65f5c687074189ac93f9894b64598278dc285d0d83.png)

First, let's express the measures of $∠AOC$ and $∠BOC,$ in terms of $x.$

Since $\overset{\to }{OD}$ is the bisector of $∠AOC,$ we have

$$
m∠AOC=2m∠DOC=2x.
$$

Since $\overset{\to }{OE}$ is the bisector of $∠BOC,$ we have

$$
m∠BOC=2m∠COE=4x+{4}^{∘}.
$$

Since $m∠AOB={130}^{∘},$ we have:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AOC+m∠BOC & =m∠AOB \\ 2x+4x+{4}^{∘} & ={130}^{∘} \\ 6x+{4}^{∘} & ={130}^{∘} \\ 6x & ={126}^{∘} \\ x & ={21}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

We are asked to find $m∠BOC.$ Substituting $x={21}^{∘}$ into the expression for $m∠BOC$ we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠BOC & =4({21}^{∘})+{4}^{∘} \\  & ={84}^{∘}+{4}^{∘} \\  & ={88}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

In the figure below, $\overset{\longrightarrow}{AC}$ is the bisector of $\angle DAB$ and $m\angle DAB = 79^\circ.$ What is the measure of $\angle DAC?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191213/assets/8d02999cf6ae7ec69fee2cdac99b8dc214c59f1ed50bbf85bec6bec01f2212ef.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
An angle bisector divides the angle into two congruent angles with equal measures, so $m\angle BAC = m\angle DAC .$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191213/assets/6e7c8ce2713441e633d7ecc3548c504d2522b4771eb6355217d6ab766a647b67.png)

Each of these congruent angles has a measure that is half the measure of the larger bisected angle. So, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠DAC & =\frac{m∠DAB}{2} \\  & =\frac{{79}^{∘}}{2} \\  & ={39.5}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating an Unknown Angle Given an Angle Bisector and Two Angle Measurements
canonical_examples.problem:
In the figure below, $\overrightarrow{OC}$ is the bisector of $\angle AOB.$ If $m \angle AOD = 90^\circ$ and $m \angle COD = 35^\circ,$ find the measure of $\angle BOD.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191213/assets/0b76c6ee6e576fa2701993e941c27f1168c213d9f5f26b1aa8a50759c3711404.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191213/assets/5ae4873418247e8d825233f903ed359ebee4d2c51ad73e6c7763102a23acded6.png)

By the angle addition postulate, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠AOC & =m∠AOD-m∠COD \\  & ={90}^{∘}-{35}^{∘} \\  & ={55}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

The bisector of an angle divides the angle into two congruent angles. Therefore,

$$
m \angle AOB =2 m \angle AOC = 110^\circ.
$$

Finally, the angle addition postulate gives

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠BOD & =m∠AOB-m∠AOD \\  & ={110}^{∘}-{90}^{∘} \\  & ={20}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating an Unknown Angle Given Two Angle Bisectors
canonical_examples.problem:
In the figure below, $\angle BAD$ is a straight angle, $\overset{\longrightarrow}{AG}$ is the bisector of $\angle CAD$ and $\overset{\longrightarrow}{AF}$ is the bisector of $\angle BAC .$ What is the measure of $\angle GAF?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191213/assets/458893f38204421326fd7dcb0693b1688eeb61fb3988e00b2d36763b47adc2d2.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191213/assets/3b0fddd3229947725b0f4f07e58ce9bfac3a9e7e348c25757162f5bc8e03d699.png)

Let $m \angle FAC=x$ and $m \angle CAG=y.$ Then,

$$
m \angle GAF=m\angle FAC + m \angle CAG=x+y.
$$

Since $\overset{\longrightarrow}{AF}$ is the bisector of $\angle BAC$, we have

$$
m \angle BAC=2x.
$$

Since $\overset{\longrightarrow}{AG}$ is the bisector of $\angle CAD$, we have

$$
m \angle CAD=2y.
$$

Finally, since $\angle BAD$ is a straight angle, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}m∠BAC+m∠CAD & =m∠BAD \\ 2x+2y & ={180}^{∘} \\ x+y & ={90}^{∘}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, $m \angle GAF=x+y=90^\circ.$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
An angle **bisector** is a line that divides an angle into two equal parts. 

For example, in the diagram below, $\overset{\longrightarrow}{AC}$ is the bisector of the angle $\angle BAD.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14191213/assets/3bf65e915f4fc26b8d87199f46ea0bc514195d857890983d31aa2d73eb38a811.png)

The resulting angles $\angle BAC$ and $\angle CAD$ are congruent (they have the same measure).
